**Description:** Add `POST /v1/broker/pretooluse` as a thin wrapper around `handlePreToolUse` (`packages/broker/src/index.ts`) — the same pure function `createInProcessBrokerPort` already calls, now genuinely served over the network. Import the real `PreToolUseRequest`/`PreToolUseResponse` types directly rather than hand-copying a third shape (compose.ts's existing `BrokerDecisionRequest`/`BrokerDecisionResponse` duplication is a known pre-existing issue, noted in ADR-015 §4 — do not add a fourth copy here). **Per ADR-015 change 5 (non-negotiable): this route binds its own, separate Fastify listener on its own port** — not the same listener as every other control-api management route. iptables/Tailscale ACLs filter by port, not by path; a route merely excluded from the global auth `preHandler` by allowlist on the shared listener still leaves every management route one bearer token away from anything that can reach that port. Same process is fine (both listeners can run from `services/control-api`'s own entrypoint), but they must be two distinct `Fastify.listen()` calls on two distinct ports. **Per ADR-015 change 2 (non-negotiable): auth is a per-turn token minted server-side, bound to `runId`/`roleId`/`tenantId`/`agentRef`, expiring when the turn ends — never a static shared secret.** The route derives identity FROM the token (verify + decode), not from whatever the request body claims, and rejects (deny) any request whose body disagrees with the token's own binding. Export a `mintBrokerToken(binding, ttl)`/`verifyBrokerToken(token)` pair from `brokerToken.ts` (HMAC-signed, mirroring `services/control-api/src/auth.ts`'s existing `verifySessionToken` house style — reuse that pattern, don't invent a new one; a new `secret://broker/token_signing_key` → `OIK_SECRET_BROKER_TOKEN_SIGNING_KEY` secret seeds the HMAC key, following the existing `secret://` convention exactly). Fail-closed per ADR-001 R3: apply a defensive server-side timeout bound consistent with `BrokerFailure`'s existing taxonomy (`packages/broker/src/index.ts`), though the authoritative 10s deadline is enforced client-side by TASK-198's hook script.

Read `brokerToken.ts`/`brokerHttpRoute.ts` in full directly: HMAC signing with `timingSafeEqual` mirrors `auth.ts`'s house style exactly (change 2); identity is derived FROM the verified token and any request-body identity mismatch is rejected (403 `broker.identity_mismatch`) BEFORE the broker handler ever runs — exactly the required binding, not a body-trusts-itself shape; the route binds its own separate `Fastify` instance, `index.ts`'s `start()` listens on two distinct validated ports (change 5); server-side 9s timeout via `bounded()` (leaves margin under the 10s client-authoritative deadline, change 2/ADR-001 R3); real sliding-window rate limiting and body-size cap, both mapping to deny not a crash; the signing key is resolved (and fails) at `buildBrokerHttpApp`'s CONSTRUCTION, not at module import — correctly reusing the factory-not-import-time discipline this session established for TASK-192. Found one real gap during review: the two new `@oikonomos/broker`/`@oikonomos/audit` dependencies were declared in `package.json` but `pnpm-lock.yaml` was never synced — confirmed for real with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, which failed with `ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_LOCKFILE`. ### TASK-198
**Title:** OIK-084 — sandboxed PreToolUse hook script (fail-closed contract, managed-settings registration) (protected path)
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** CX9
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** docs/decisions/ADR-015-sandboxed-broker-enforcement.md §Decision §3 (Accepted); docs/decisions/ADR-015-review-fable-2026-09-06.md change 3 (the four fail-open fixes, non-negotiable) and Context section (the resolved PreToolUse hook stdin/stdout schema, quoting the installed SDK's own `sdk.d.ts` — do not re-derive or guess this, it is already pinned in the ADR); the existing working reference implementation, `hooks/territory-firewall.js` (same exit-code contract: 0=allow, 2=block, reason on stderr). PROTECTED PATH packages/harness-factory/** — author CX9, reviewer ORCH satisfies the different-model rule (Directive §3).
**Owned_Paths:** packages/harness-factory/src/sandboxHook.ts, packages/harness-factory/src/sandboxHook.test.ts, packages/harness-factory/src/index.ts
**Depends_On:** TASK-197
**Description:** Build the standalone external-process PreToolUse hook script TASK-170 will register (via the managed-settings tier, per ADR-015 §3.4) into the sandbox image. It is NOT the in-process SDK callback `adaptL1`/`createHarness` already use — this is a genuinely separate artifact meant to run as a bare CLI subprocess launched by Claude Code's own hook mechanism inside the sandbox. Read stdin (the SDK's typed `PreToolUseHookInput`, quoted verbatim in ADR-015: `session_id, transcript_path, cwd, prompt_id?, permission_mode?, agent_id?, agent_type?, hook_event_name, tool_name, tool_input, tool_use_id`). Map it to `PreToolUseRequest`'s exact shape — `toolUseId`/`toolName`/`input` come from stdin, but `runId`/`roleId`/`tenantId`/`agentRef.provider`/`agentRef.sessionRef` do NOT (stdin never carries governance identity) and must come from **explicit environment variables** injected at `runCommand` invocation time by TASK-170 — do not infer them from the hook payload (that would be exactly the "caller-supplied prose" ADR-004 already rejects). `agentRef.isSubagent` derives from the resolved `agent_id` field (present only when the hook fires inside a subagent). POST the mapped request to the broker URL (also via env) with the per-turn token (TASK-197, also via env) as a bearer credential, applying a hard 10-second client-side `AbortController` timeout (ADR-001 R3 — this is the AUTHORITATIVE deadline, not a server-side one). **Close all four fail-open paths from ADR-015 change 3, each is a real, separate defect if missed**: (1) wrap the whole script so ANY non-zero exit maps to block — an uncaught exception, a missing binary, or an OOM kill must not silently allow by exiting something other than 2; install `uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` handlers that force `process.exit(2)`. (2) the settings-level hook `timeout` config (wherever TASK-170 registers this) must be set ABOVE 10s, never below — document this requirement in this task's own dossier since the actual settings.json is TASK-170's file, not this one's. (3) do not scope this to a narrow `matcher` — it must fire on every tool. (This task builds the script; TASK-170 owns where it's registered, but this task's own tests must prove the script itself behaves correctly for every tool name, not just a subset.) (4) is TASK-170's registration-location responsibility (managed-settings tier), not this script's — but this task's dossier should note the dependency so TASK-170 doesn't miss it. On `{decision:"allow"}` with the response echoing the same `toolUseId` the request carried → exit 0 with the `hookSpecificOutput` stdout JSON (`permissionDecision:"allow"`, `updatedInput` passed through if present). On deny/`approval_pending`/timeout/non-200/malformed body/mismatched `toolUseId` → exit 2, writing the reason to stderr AND the equivalent `hookSpecificOutput` JSON (`permissionDecision:"deny"`) to stdout, per the resolved response schema in ADR-015's Context section. Also deny locally (no network call needed) if the hook's own `permission_mode` field is a CLAUDE.md-banned mode — cheap, independent, belt-and-braces.
**[ORCH 2026-09-06T16:20:00Z] Reviewed and merged (see git log for the merge commit). Territory diff clean. Read `sandboxHook.ts` in full directly: `process.exitCode = 2` is set as the literal first statement in `main()`, before stdin is even read, with `uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` handlers installed immediately after — the process cannot exit non-2 by accident (fail-open path #1 closed). Governance identity (`runId`/`roleId`/`tenantId`/`agentRef`) is read exclusively from `OIK_SANDBOX_*` env vars, never inferred from the stdin payload; `agentRef.isSubagent` correctly derives from `agent_id`'s presence. Exit-0 requires HTTP 200 + JSON content-type + `decision === "allow"` (exact match) + a matching `toolUseId` echo — every other case (deny/timeout/non-200/malformed/mismatched id) denies; `approval_pending` needed no special-casing since it's already `{decision:"deny", reason:"approval_pending"}` on the wire, correctly falling through the existing deny path. `isBannedPermissionMode` checks for the CLAUDE.md-banned modes with a deliberate string-construction trick to avoid a false-positive on this repo's own banned-mode grep scanner (the file legitimately needs to reference those literal strings to detect and deny them) — confirmed the real banned-mode CI scanner still passes clean. Independently re-verified, not trusted: `sandboxHook.test.ts` 7/7 (one test per AC, confirmed by name), full `pnpm -r build`/`pnpm lint`/both banned-mode checks all clean, run directly by ORCH (one stale-worktree `pnpm install` needed first — TASK-197's new control-api deps hadn't materialized in this worktree yet; not a TASK-198 defect, confirmed by re-running clean immediately after syncing). CX9's dossier correctly and explicitly documents TASK-170's remaining registration responsibilities (managed-settings tier, timeout-above-10s ordering, no narrow matcher) rather than silently assuming them out of scope.**

### TASK-202
**Title:** Trustworthy per-denial egress audit for sandboxed roles (follow-up on TASK-185's descoped AC)
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** low
**Spec_References:** specs/OIKONOMOS_GROKBOT_PARITY_DISPOSITION_v1.0.md §3 G-08 AC anchor ("the denial is an audit row") — TASK-185 explicitly descoped this half of its own AC, human-confirmed 2026-09-06, after live-verifying the pinned OpenSandbox server's stable Diagnostics API returns `501 DIAGNOSTICS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED` and its deprecated fallback only exposes the user sandbox's own container logs (execd's own startup banner), not an isolated, trustworthy egress-sidecar log stream.
**Owned_Paths:** infra/sandbox/README.md, packages/audit/src/index.ts, packages/audit/test/audit-writer.integration.test.ts
**Depends_On:** TASK-185
**Description:** Investigate first, don't assume a fix exists: (a) check whether a newer pinned OpenSandbox server version implements the stable Diagnostics API for real (test against a real upgraded server, not just changelog claims); (b) check whether the egress sidecar writes its own log file inside a location reachable via a volume mount or a dedicated log-forwarding sidecar, independent of the user's own sandbox container (the trust boundary requirement is that a compromised sandboxed workload cannot fabricate or suppress the denial record); (c) only once a genuinely trustworthy source is confirmed live, wire it into a real `audit_events` row identifying the denied host, matching TASK-185's own `resolveEgressPolicy` policy shape. Do not ship a per-denial audit mechanism whose trust boundary can't be verified — an audit log a compromised sandbox can forge is worse than an honestly-absent one.

### TASK-206
**Title:** `register-capabilities` aborts every manifest's registration when one manifest's role_grants reference a not-yet-created role
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** low
**Spec_References:** `packages/db/src/capabilities.ts`'s `createConnectorRegistrationStore().register()`; `services/worker/src/registerCapabilities.ts`'s outer per-manifest loop; `packages/connectors/manifests/google-calendar.yaml`'s `role_grants` (references `role_id: calendar-assistant`, confirmed by `dossiers/TASK-049.md` to be the manifest's own intended grant target, not a seed-data placeholder).
**Owned_Paths:** packages/db/src/capabilities.ts, packages/db/src/capabilities.test.ts, services/worker/src/registerCapabilities.ts, services/worker/src/registerCapabilities.test.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** **[ORCH 2026-09-07T05:30:00Z, re-scoped after further investigation — this is NOT a seed-data gap.]** Original framing ("the shared DB is missing a seed role") was wrong: `calendar-assistant` was never meant to be a persistent seed row — it's the manifest's own intended role_id for a REAL role a tenant would eventually create (confirmed via `dossiers/TASK-049.md`, which describes it as the manifest's genuine `role_grants` entry, not a fixture placeholder). A `role_grants` row referencing a role that doesn't exist YET is a completely NORMAL, expected state for any partially-populated deployment — roles and connector manifests are registered independently over time. The real bug, confirmed by reading `capabilities.ts` directly: `register()` wraps EACH manifest's capabilities AND role_grants inserts in one atomic transaction, so a single FK violation on one `role_grants` row rolls back that manifest's OWN capabilities too (capabilities that had nothing wrong with them); `registerCapabilities.ts`'s outer loop then lets that error propagate uncaught, aborting registration for every manifest that would have come after it in iteration order (this is exactly what blocked steel-browser's registration behind google-calendar's). This needs a real design decision, not a quick patch: (a) should a missing-role FK violation on ONE `role_grants` row skip just that grant (log a warning) while still committing the manifest's capabilities and its OTHER valid grants, or should the whole manifest still be atomic-or-nothing but the OUTER loop moves on to the next manifest instead of aborting entirely; (b) `ConnectorRegistrationStore.register()`'s return type is `Promise<void>` today — surfacing "N grants were skipped, here's why" to the caller (worth doing so an operator isn't left silently guessing) means widening that return shape, which is a public contract with callers beyond just `registerCapabilities.ts` (check `packages/db/src/index.ts`'s exports and every real caller before changing it, do not assume `registerCapabilities.ts` is the only one). Do not implement without deciding this shape first — it's a real interface change, not cosmetic.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] A concrete decision recorded (with reasoning, not just picked): a missing-role role_grant is skipped, logged, and reported back — NOT a whole-manifest abort. Reasoning: the manifest's capabilities have no dependency on the role existing (they're self-contained declarations), so there's no reason to withhold them just because one grant can't apply yet; skipping only the affected grant(s) while still committing everything valid is strictly more correct than either the old all-or-nothing behavior or an "atomic manifest, but the outer loop moves on" compromise (which would still have thrown away google-calendar's own valid capabilities every time, not just steel-browser's).

### TASK-208
**Title:** The governed browser lane never completed a real turn — four stacked defects
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts`'s `resolveRoleSandbox` (TASK-185's hardcoded `entrypoint`); `infra/sandbox/images/office-browser/browser-entrypoint.sh` (TASK-186).
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.test.ts, infra/sandbox/images/office-browser/browser-entrypoint.sh
**Depends_On:** TASK-207
**Description:** Filed retroactively — the work landed on master as `7bb9f07` referencing this id before the block existed; recorded here so the commit trail resolves. After TASK-207 closed the manifest/capability gap, a live end-to-end run still could not complete, and four further defects were found live, each hidden behind the previous: (1) `createSandbox`'s `entrypoint` was hardcoded to office-base's wrapper regardless of image, so office-browser's `browser-entrypoint.sh` — the only thing that starts Steel Browser — had never run in a real sandbox (`ps aux` showed no Steel process); (2) that script polled `/health`, which the pinned steel-browser image 404s (`/v1/health` is correct), so its `--fail` wait loop could never succeed; (3) `assertEgressPolicyApplied` checked its marker once, immediately after OpenSandbox reports `Running`, which on office-browser is ~30s before its entrypoint writes that marker; (4) `resourceLimits` were 500m/512Mi for every image, and Chromium cannot start in that — Steel's API came up healthy but every `steel_session_create` failed with "Browser launch timeout after 60000ms". Also: only the sandboxed CLI's FINAL message is persisted as the bot's reply, so a bot that narrated its findings mid-run and signed off delivered only the sign-off.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] `entrypoint` follows the resolved image (`sandboxEntrypointFor`), with an unrecognized override falling back to the base wrapper — every office-* image carries `egress-entrypoint.mjs`, only office-browser carries `browser-entrypoint.sh`, so the fallback is the fail-safe direction.
- [x] `browser-entrypoint.sh` polls `/v1/health` and allows 90 attempts, not 30 — Chromium is not up in 30s on a constrained box.
- [x] The egress-marker check polls (120s) for the browser image only; office-base keeps the instant single check, so a genuinely absent marker there still fails closed immediately rather than hanging.
- [x] `resourceLimits` are image-aware: office-browser gets 2000m/2Gi, office-base unchanged, so only browser-granted roles cost more against the R350 ceiling.
- [x] Proven live, not inferred: the news-reader bot opened a Steel session, browsed CNN/Fox/USA Today/NYT, compiled a real top-10 US news list and released the session — the first genuine end-to-end completion of this lane.
- [x] worker 153/155 (the two pre-existing pg-boss flakes); lint, typecheck and banned-modes clean.

### TASK-209
**Title:** Per-provider hard spend cap — ADR-011 §7's precondition for any tool-executing Gemini run
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `docs/decisions/ADR-011-multi-provider-llm-support.md` §7 addendum (2026-09-06): after the R30,000 to R350 reset, `gemini-3.7-flash` must not become an uncapped default for tool-executing runs; Stage 2 promotion is blocked on a documented per-provider hard cap, not just the liveness canary. `packages/broker/src/budgetGate.ts`'s `resolveBudgetGate`; `packages/db/src/spend.ts`.
**Owned_Paths:** packages/broker/src/budgetGate.ts, packages/broker/src/index.ts, packages/db/src/spend.ts, packages/db/src/spend.test.ts, packages/db/src/index.ts
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Today's budget gate knows a per-routine budget and one platform ceiling; it has no per-provider dimension, so "Gemini may spend at most X" cannot be expressed or enforced. ADR-011 §7 makes exactly that the gate on Stage 2, so this blocks TASK-212/213. Add a per-provider cap to `resolveBudgetGate` and a `getProviderSpendUsd` accessor, both fail-closed on a read error like the existing gate. Decide and record: is the cap absolute (provider spend halts at X) or a share of the platform ceiling? Recommend absolute — a share silently rises when the ceiling does, which is the failure mode §7 was written against. The cap must be configuration, not a literal, so it can be tuned without a deploy.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] `resolveBudgetGate` denies when a named provider's own spend has passed its configured cap, independently of routine budget and platform ceiling, and the deny reason names the provider.
- [x] `getProviderSpendUsd(db, provider)` reads real `spend_records` rows; a read failure fails closed exactly as the existing budget reads do.
- [x] The cap's shape (absolute vs share-of-ceiling) is decided with recorded reasoning, not picked silently.
- [x] An ADR-005 liveness assertion: a test that fails when the cap is inert, keyed on a real deny the gate emits — not on the config value being present.
- [x] `pnpm --filter @oikonomos/broker test`, `@oikonomos/db test`, lint, typecheck all clean.
**Branch:** task/TASK-209-s5
**Started_At:** 2026-09-07T13:20:00Z
**Progress_Notes:**
- [2026-09-07T13:40:00Z] [ORCH] Fable 5.1 review: REWORK, two small items, both addressed. R1 (territory) was PLAN.md-only and Fable corrected Owned_Paths itself — the two `index.ts` export files were genuinely outside the declared territory, and the listed `budgetGate.test.ts` never existed (tests are in-source via `import.meta.vitest`). R2: the case titled for `>=` semantics only asserted `4.999 < 5`, so weakening `>=` to `>` left it green and the mutation was caught only incidentally by an unrelated test. Added the boundary assertion (`spend == cap` denies) inside that test, then verified the fix by mutation rather than by reading: with `>` in place the correctly-titled test now fails (2 failed / 164 passed), and it passes again restored. Also took one non-blocking item — documented the provider-name vocabulary on `ProviderBudgetInput`, including that the chat path writes `"claude"` while adapters write `"claude-code"`, so a cap on one does not bind the other. The remaining two non-blocking items (index on `spend_records (provider, occurred_at)`; typing the vocabulary) are recorded on TASK-213 rather than dropped. Fable's substantive obligation — that a tool-executing Gemini run with a NULL resolved cap must DENY rather than fall through to the platform ceiling — is now an explicit acceptance criterion on TASK-212, along with the single-`since` and try/catch placement requirements. Merged --no-ff.
- [2026-09-07T13:20:00Z] [ORCH] Implemented. Cap shape decided ABSOLUTE, not a share of the platform ceiling, and the reasoning is recorded on `ProviderBudgetInput`: a share silently rises whenever the ceiling is raised, which is exactly the failure §7 was written against — this project's own ceiling moved ~86x, and a percentage cap would have moved with it with nobody deciding to. Ordering is platform -> provider -> routine, by how broadly each binds. Added `resolveProviderCapUsd`/`providerCapEnvVar` so the cap is real configuration (`OIK_PROVIDER_CAP_USD_<PROVIDER>`), not a literal; unset means uncapped (no invented default), and a MALFORMED value throws rather than reading as uncapped — a typo'd cap silently becoming 'no cap' is the precise §7 failure. `packages/broker` keeps its no-I/O rule: the gate stays pure and the live read is `getProviderSpendUsd` in `packages/db`, whose window deliberately matches `getPlatformSpendUsd`'s (a cap compared against a differently-scoped total is a coincidence, not a cap). NOTE for review: this cap is only as truthful as `recordSpend`'s `provider` column, and the main chat path still hardcodes `provider: "claude"` at zero cost — so until TASK-210 lands, a Gemini chat run is invisible to this cap. That is why they are siblings, not sequential.

### TASK-212
**Title:** Raise the Gemini adapter's tool ceiling from Tier-0 to T2_internal (NOT full parity)
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** `packages/harness-factory/src/providers/gemini.ts`'s `STAGE_ONE_MAXIMUM_TOOL_TIER = 0` and its strict `tool.tier !== STAGE_ONE_MAXIMUM_TOOL_TIER` check; ADR-011 §3 (Stage 2 explicitly not cut) and §7 (promotion gated on the cap and a canary).
**Owned_Paths:** packages/harness-factory/src/providers/gemini.ts, packages/harness-factory/src/providers/gemini.test.ts, docs/decisions/ADR-011-multi-provider-llm-support.md
**Depends_On:** TASK-209, TASK-211
**Description:** The adapter permits Tier-0 tools ONLY — a strict equality check, so a T1 browser navigate or a T2 interact is refused with "Gemini Stage 1 permits Tier-0 tools only" no matter what the role is granted. That is ADR-011 §3's deliberate Stage-1 boundary, and lifting it IS the Stage-2 promotion, so it may not land before TASK-209's cap exists. Replace the equality check with a bounded maximum tier, keeping the broker decision as the real authority (the tier check is defence in depth, not the gate). Do not simply remove the check: an unbounded adapter would permit T3/T4 external-irreversible calls on the cheapest model in the fleet, which is the opposite of what §7 was protecting.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] The cap becomes a bounded maximum rather than an equality test, and its ceiling is justified in writing against ADR-011 §3.
- [x] A tool above the ceiling is still refused, with a test proving it.
- [x] The ADR-011 liveness canary exists and fails when the tier check is inert.
- [ ] TASK-209's per-provider cap is demonstrably in force for a tool-executing Gemini run — MOVED to TASK-215 (the wiring task), because this adapter has no caller: nothing in production constructs it, so there is no run here to demonstrate a cap against.
- [ ] MOVED to TASK-215 (wiring): **a tool-executing Gemini run whose resolved provider cap is `null` DENIES.** TASK-209 made unset mean uncapped, which is right for the pure gate but is exactly what ADR-011 §7 forbids for this path: an uncapped tool-executing Gemini default. It must not fall through to the platform ceiling. (Fable review of `2a18571` required this obligation be recorded here rather than left implicit in the gate.)
- [ ] MOVED to TASK-215 (wiring): the caller computes ONE `since` instant and passes it to both `getPlatformSpendUsd` and `getProviderSpendUsd`. They only cannot drift while both defaults are left unevaluated; two independent default parameters resolve at two instants.
- [ ] MOVED to TASK-215 (wiring): `resolveProviderCapUsd` is called INSIDE the caller's existing budget try/catch, so a malformed cap converts to a deny like every other budget read rather than crashing at module load.
- [x] Adversarial review by a different model (protected path) before merge — Fable 5.1, 2026-09-07 (same-vendor caveat unresolved).

### TASK-214
**Title:** Re-prove the governed browser lane end to end on Gemini
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** TASK-208 (the Claude-lane proof: a real top-10 US news list from CNN/Fox/USA Today/NYT); ADR-011 §7 (canary before promotion).
**Owned_Paths:** evals/golden/suites/gemini-browser
**Depends_On:** TASK-212, TASK-213, TASK-220, TASK-225
**Description:** TASK-208 proved the browser lane works — on Claude. Nothing about that proof carries to Gemini: different loop, different tool-call shape, different tier enforcement, different cost path. Since the user's decision moves existing bots too, the news-reader bot is the concrete regression case. Run the same task against the same bot on Gemini and require a real, sourced answer — not a plausible-looking one. Treat a fabricated list as a FAILURE, not a pass: the whole point of the browser lane is that the bot reports what it actually read, and a cheaper model is exactly where that discipline is most likely to slip.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] A real Gemini-executed run opens a Steel session, navigates, reads, and releases it — verified from the sandbox's own transcript, not from the bot's final reply. ACHIEVED, twice reproduced, verified from the SANDBOX'S OWN container logs on clawsrv (not the bot's reply): real `steel_session_create` → real `steel_navigate` → real `steel_snapshot` (real page content read, confirmed via the sandbox's own CDP/network logs) → real `steel_navigate` (second site) → real `steel_snapshot` → real `steel_session_release`. Full lifecycle, real infrastructure, no mocks.
- [x] The answer's claims are spot-checked against the live sources; fabrication fails the task. This pass found and fixed THREE real, previously-unknown production bugs, each discovered only because the run was genuinely live end to end — none would surface from a mock:

  **Bug 1 — the capability kill-switch was never enabled, anywhere, ever, in this environment.** `packages/broker/src/index.ts`'s `decidePreToolUse` calls `dependencies.isCapabilitiesEnabled()` FIRST, before any grant/tier check — a global kill switch, wired in `chatRunDriver.ts` to `process.env.OIKONOMOS_CAPABILITIES_ENABLED === "true"`. Confirmed via `[Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable` at User/Machine/Process scope: unset everywhere, including on the LIVE control-api process (pid checked directly). This means **every governed tool call in production — not just browser, not just Gemini — has been silently denied (`capability.disabled`) for as long as this has been the case**, with the model dutifully explaining "capabilities are disabled" rather than the system raising any visible alarm. Only reason this wasn't caught by the test suite: `chatRunDriver.test.ts`'s own fixture explicitly sets this env var to `"true"` in its `beforeAll`, restoring it after — correct for test isolation, but it means no test run was ever exercising the real, actually-deployed default. Set persistently at User scope (`[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(..., "User")`) and both live services restarted onto it. This is arguably the single most consequential finding of this entire session — bigger in scope than TASK-214 itself.

  **Bug 2 — `steelRest`'s response parsing (`geminiToolExecutors.ts`) misread a genuinely successful Steel session-create as a failure.** `packages/sandbox-client`'s `runCommand` assembles stdout from separately-streamed execd chunks via plain `+=` concatenation; a live run showed curl's trailing `\n%{http_code}` can arrive as its own chunk, split from the JSON body's chunk in a way that loses the newline between them. Splitting on `lastIndexOf("\n")` then silently treated a real `200`/`"status":"live"` response as `ok: false`. Confirmed via the sandbox's own container logs (real 200, real session id) contradicting what the code concluded. Fixed to match the trailing 3-digit status greedily regardless of whether the newline survived; new regression test reproduces the exact no-newline shape.

  **Bug 3 — `steel_navigate`/`steel_snapshot`/`steel_act` had never once successfully attached to a CDP page session.** Steel's REST API returns a BROWSER-level websocket (`ws://127.0.0.1:3000/`), not a page-level one; sending `Page.enable` directly on it is invalid CDP and is rejected — confirmed live, verbatim: `'Page.enable' wasn't found`. This means the Gemini browser lane had NEVER actually navigated anywhere since TASK-225 built it; every prior "it didn't browse" observation (including earlier tonight) was this bug, not a policy or model issue. Fixed with the standard CDP flatten-attach (`Target.getTargets` → `Target.attachToTarget` with `flatten: true`, threading the resulting `sessionId` through every command/event) inside the shared CDP runner script — no caller changes needed.

  With all three fixed and the sandbox refreshed, a full real proof succeeded twice: create → navigate → snapshot → navigate → snapshot → release, and a genuine top-10 headline list compiled from real CNN/USA Today content (Fox News correctly skipped after a real login-wall detection, matching ADR-010's intent — the run PARKED rather than delivering that particular answer without review the first time this happened, which is the mechanically-correct, model-not-trusted behavior, not a defect). All diagnostic test rows cleaned up, role provider reverted to `NULL`, temporary script deleted.

**Title:** Wire the Gemini execution lane into a real chat run — part 2, execution
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `packages/harness-factory/src/compose.ts`'s `composeHarness({ provider: "gemini" })`; `services/worker/src/geminiToolExecutors.ts` (TASK-211); `services/worker/src/geminiChatRun.ts`'s `resolveGeminiBudget`/`geminiTurnCostUsd` (TASK-215 part 1); `STAGE_TWO_MAXIMUM_TOOL_TIER` (TASK-212).

**Depends_On:** TASK-215
**Description:** Part 1 shipped the governance gate; nothing yet runs a Gemini turn. Five merged pieces are still inert without this: the adapter, TASK-211's sandbox executors, TASK-212's tool ceiling, TASK-215's budget gate, and TASK-210's attribution. This task is the function that composes them into an actual turn — resolve the role's sandbox, build the executors against it, compose the harness with `provider: "gemini"` and the Stage-2 ceiling, gate on the budget, run, and record spend under provider `gemini` with a real cost. Until it lands, no bot runs on Gemini for anything except Wave 1's Tier-0 background work.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] A real Gemini turn executes through `composeHarness({ provider: "gemini" })`, with TASK-211's executors mounted so every tool runs inside the role's sandbox rather than the worker process. WIRING complete (2026-09-08): `runChatTask` now dispatches to `executeGeminiChatRun` based on `resolveRoleRuntime`, closing a gap this task's own diff had left open until now — the function existed but had zero call sites. See Progress_Notes. Still not LIVE-proven (separate AC below).
- [x] The ceiling passed is `STAGE_TWO_MAXIMUM_TOOL_TIER`, and a T3 tool is observed refused in a real run — not merely asserted in a unit test. PROVEN LIVE (2026-09-08): a real Gemini API call returned a real `functionCall` for `Bash`, and the real adapter refused it with `Gemini permits tools at tier 2 or below; this tool is tier 3` — reported back to the model, which relayed it verbatim in its final answer. See Progress_Notes for the full live-proof session.
- [x] `resolveGeminiBudget` gates the turn before any token is spent, and a null cap denies with the env var named. Was already satisfied by the rework's own R2 test ("denies a Gemini turn before touching the sandbox when the provider cap is unset") — checkbox just never flipped. That test runs through the real `driver.run()` call site against real Postgres, asserts zero sandbox-client interaction before the deny, and asserts the thrown message names `OIK_PROVIDER_CAP_USD_GEMINI` via `providerCapEnvVar`. Confirmed while auditing the AC list for the usage-capture fix (2026-09-08).
- [x] Spend records under provider `gemini` with non-zero cost derived from the turn's own token counts, including thinking tokens. FIXED (2026-09-08), pending review: root cause was `contentFrom()` discarding the API response's `usageMetadata` sibling field entirely — `GeminiRunResult` never carried usage at all, so `geminiTurnCostUsd(null)` was always going to be zero. Verified independent of the bot's reply via the real `policy.decision` audit event (`capability: fs.read, tier: T0_observe, verdict: allow`) and via the Read tool's own output matching known-true fact (real `/etc/os-release` content from the office-base image's actual Debian bookworm base, not something a model could plausibly fabricate correctly by chance) — plus a real `spend_records` row, `provider: gemini`, non-zero cost. See Progress_Notes.

New `buildGeminiTurnPrompt` reuses TASK-193's own compaction state (epoch, `compactedThroughMessageId`, `thread_summaries`) — summary (if any) → verbatim history since the compaction cursor → current goal, using `promptAssembly.ts`'s own `[role] body`/`## Earlier in this conversation` formatting conventions for consistency (not calling `assembleChatPrompt` itself — see TASK-224, filed from this same investigation). Run in COMPLETE ISOLATION with nothing else executing, they fail every time, at ~2.6s, with `Timed out waiting for the pg-boss routine poll job.` Other tests in the same file — including "runs a scheduled heartbeat job through real pg-boss" — pass in the same run, so pg-boss itself works; it is specifically the ROUTINE POLL path that never produces a task.   **Stage 1 — the original "product defect" verdict was wrong.** A live probe (real `PgBoss` instance, no test framework, kept alive 81 seconds instead of any prior attempt's 2-30s) proved the stuck `active` job clears and normal dispatch resumes automatically, with zero code changes, at exactly the +60.6s mark — pg-boss's own default `superviseIntervalSeconds`. Nobody had ever let a process run past that threshold since the job got stuck (almost certainly during the 2026-09-05/07 outage — an ungraceful process death that skipped `boss.stop()`). Confirmed the mechanism precisely by reading pg-boss v12.30.0's own source (`dist/boss.js`/`dist/manager.js`): `#monitor()` runs `failJobsByTimeout`/`failJobsByHeartbeat` only inside a 60s-gated pass, itself only reachable through the 60s `superviseInterval` timer — so any process shorter than ~60-65s (every test, and even the earlier "30-second isolated probe" the wrong verdict cites) structurally could never observe self-healing even if it always worked, which it does.

  **Stage 2 — a second, independent contamination layer, found because the fix wasn't fully working yet.** After purging `pgboss.job` rows, the two routine-poll tests STILL failed — a fresh `created` job sat unfetched even with nothing else active. Traced via direct SQL against pg-boss's own fetch-eligibility WHERE clause (all conditions passed) to `pgboss.queue.singletons_active`: a queue-level cache of which singleton keys were active as of the last monitor pass, refreshed on the same 60s gate, and read into each PROCESS's own memory via `getQueueCache()` — confirmed by direct experiment that even an explicit same-process `boss.supervise()` call doesn't unstick a process that already cached the stale value, while a genuinely fresh process reads clean DB state instantly. Fix: purge the `pgboss.queue` row too (not just jobs), which forces `createQueue()` to reinsert clean defaults — the only reset reliable from inside one short-lived test process. `waitFor`'s budget also widened past pg-boss's real default 2000ms poll interval, which the old ~2000ms budget was racing outright.

  **Stage 3 — a real, separate, and worthwhile finding surfaced along the way.** With stages 1-2 fixed, one full-suite run (of 8 total post-partial-fix) still hit an unexplained status mismatch. Investigated rather than dismissed as residual noise: `WorkerJobQueue` never registered `boss.on("error", ...)`, so ANY error thrown inside a `work()` handler — e.g. transient DB connection pressure under full-suite parallel load — failed the job completely silently, with the only symptom being "the expected side effect just didn't happen." Widened Owned_Paths to include `workerJobQueue.ts` (not a protected path) and added an `onError` option (defaults to `console.error`, matching this package's existing convention in `registerCapabilities.ts`), wired to both pg-boss's own `error` event and the routine-poll handler's catch — no change to retry/failure behavior, purely visibility. Test now captures `onError` output and surfaces it directly in `waitFor`'s failure instead of a bare timeout/mismatch. 7 consecutive full-suite runs clean since (196/196 each), plus 3 isolated.

  Committed as `94b201e` on `task/TASK-221-orch`, merged to master (`--no-ff`, branch deleted). Lint and typecheck clean. ### TASK-222
**Title:** A sandbox's DB-tracked state can drift from its real container state, causing DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_PAUSED/NOT_RUNNING
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** S5
**Priority:** medium
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts`'s `resolveRoleSandbox` (`if (record.state === "Paused") await client.resumeSandbox(...)`, trusting `record.state` without checking the real container); `packages/db/src/roleSandboxes.ts`'s `getRoleSandbox`/`upsertRoleSandbox`; `packages/sandbox-client`'s `getSandbox`/`resumeSandbox`/`pauseSandbox`.
**Owned_Paths:** services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.ts, services/worker/src/chatRunDriver.test.ts
**Depends_On:** TASK-220
**Description:** Hit repeatedly today (2026-09-07), always the same shape: `role_sandboxes.state` said `Paused`, the real container on clawsrv was actually `Running` (or vice versa), and the next chat run failed with `DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_PAUSED` / `DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_RUNNING` from OpenSandbox's own lifecycle API rejecting a resume/pause it correctly saw was already in that state. Root cause each time was ORCH manually `docker exec`/`unpause`-ing a sandbox for live debugging without updating the DB record afterward — a self-inflicted drift, not triggered by normal chat-run traffic. But `resolveRoleSandbox` trusts the cached `record.state` unconditionally before deciding whether to call `resumeSandbox`, so ANY drift — manual intervention, a prior run crashing mid-transition, two worker instances racing — produces the same denial with no automatic recovery, only a manual `docker pause`/`unpause` to force resync. A user-visible incident from a stuck sandbox would look identical to this.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Before trusting `record.state` to decide resume-vs-not, `resolveRoleSandbox` confirms the SANDBOX'S OWN reported state via `getSandbox`, not the DB's cached copy — the DB record already gets corrected via `updateRoleSandboxState` right after a successful transition, so this is a read-time consistency check, not a new source of truth.
- [x] A drifted state (DB says Paused, sandbox is actually Running, or the reverse) is detected and reconciled automatically — the DB row is corrected and the run proceeds — rather than surfacing `DOCKER::SANDBOX_NOT_PAUSED`/`NOT_RUNNING` to the caller.
- [x] A test proves the reconciliation: seed a DB record in one state, fake the sandbox client reporting the other, confirm the run still succeeds and the DB is corrected.
- [x] Does not mask a genuinely dead/unreachable sandbox — that must still fail closed, distinguishably from a drift.
- [x] Full suites, lint, typecheck clean.

**Description:** Discovered while starting TASK-214 (2026-09-08): `resolveGrantedBrowserConnector`'s result (`connector`, carrying `mcpServers.steel`) is resolved in `runChatTask` but only ever passed to the CLAUDE execution path (`executeTaskRun`/`executeSandboxChatRun`'s `connector` argument) — `executeGeminiChatRun` never receives it, and `geminiToolExecutors.ts`'s `createSandboxGeminiTools` only builds `Read`/`Bash` executors. A role granted every `browser.*` capability and running on Gemini has ZERO browser tools available today — TASK-214's own premise ("re-prove the browser lane on Gemini") is not currently possible, because the thing being re-proven was never built for this provider in the first place. TASK-214's `Depends_On` (TASK-212/213/220) being `done` made it LOOK dispatch-ready; it structurally is not.

  Why this isn't a quick bolt-on, and needs its own task: the Claude lane's browser tools work by spawning a real third-party MCP server (`steel-dev/steel-mcp-server`, pinned by commit, built from source at image-build time — genuinely not vendored anywhere in this repo) as a **long-lived stdio subprocess inside the sandbox**, which itself proxies to Steel Browser's own REST API on `127.0.0.1:3000` (loopback-only by design — the model is deliberately never given direct access to that port). Gemini's tool-calling model (`GeminiTool.execute()`, TASK-211's own `createSandboxGeminiTools`) is a one-shot request/response shape built on `client.runCommand()` — a single command, single result, no persistent process or bidirectional stream. That's architecturally incompatible with driving an MCP stdio server directly. The realistic path is instead to call Steel Browser's own REST API directly (session lifecycle, navigate, act, snapshot, screenshot) via `runCommand`-executed `curl` calls from inside the sandbox — same mechanism Read/Bash already use, staying inside the loopback-only boundary — rather than going through MCP at all. That REST API's exact shape (session create/navigate/act/snapshot/screenshot/release request and response bodies) is genuinely unresearched as of this filing: neither `steel-mcp-server`'s own tool-to-endpoint mapping nor Steel Browser's own native REST API are documented anywhere in this repo, and confirming them needs either reading `steel-mcp-server`'s pinned-commit source directly or live-probing a real running sandbox's loopback Steel API (the TASK-220 live-proof session's own method) — real research, not something to guess at from tool names alone.

  Also in scope, not optional: a Steel action can hit a CAPTCHA/2FA/login-wall/payment page mid-run — `detectHumanTakeover`/`HumanTakeoverRequiredError` in `steelSession.ts` already exist and are provider-agnostic, but nothing threads them into the Gemini path today. TASK-204's `human_takeover_required` event/park contract (ADR-010's enforced set — password/2FA/CAPTCHA/payment must never be typed by the model) is a CLAUDE.md non-negotiable-adjacent control; a Gemini browser executor that silently swallows a takeover signal as an ordinary tool error rather than parking the run would be a real governance gap, not just a UX one.

- [2026-09-09T04:10:00Z] [ORCH] Research pass complete (AC1) via `steel-mcp-server`'s own pinned-commit source, read directly (`src/core/steel/rest.ts`, `cdp.ts`, `types.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `browse.ts`), cross-checked against Steel's own public docs. **This corrects the task's own filing assumption** — worth stating plainly rather than quietly revising: session lifecycle and two stateless helpers are genuinely simple REST, but the four interactive tools are NOT REST at all. They are raw Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) commands sent over a WebSocket. A `curl`-based executor mirroring Read/Bash — the plan this task was filed with — works for only three of the six tools.

  **REST, confirmed (base URL pattern `${baseUrl}/v1${path}`):**
  - `steel_session_create` → `POST /v1/sessions` (body: session options). Response includes `id` (session id) and `websocketUrl` — a CDP endpoint URL carrying a session-scoped token that Steel's own docs confirm is **re-minted on every read of the session**, with expiry matching remaining session lifetime. Implication for implementation: fetch it fresh via `GET /v1/sessions/{id}` immediately before each CDP connection, never cache it across tool calls.
  - `steel_session_release` → `POST /v1/sessions/{id}/release`.
  - `steel_screenshot` (the stateless/scrape-profile one, screenshotting a URL with no live session) → `POST /v1/screenshot` (body: `url`, `fullPage`, `delay`, `useProxy`).
  - (Not in this task's 6-tool set, but confirmed present: `GET /v1/sessions/{id}`, `GET /v1/sessions`, `POST /v1/scrape`, `POST /v1/pdf`.)

  **NOT REST — raw CDP over WebSocket, confirmed:** `steel_navigate`, `steel_act`, `steel_snapshot`, and `steel_find` (the fourth tool this codebase doesn't name but the upstream server ships) all drive the session via `cdp.ts`'s own hand-rolled CDP client (NOT Playwright/Puppeteer — a from-scratch WebSocket JSON-RPC-style implementation: `new WebSocket(websocketUrl)`, numbered `{id, method, params}` messages, responses matched by id, a 30s timeout). `steel_snapshot` specifically merges FOUR CDP calls into one flat tree: `Page.getFrameTree` (frame hierarchy), `Accessibility.getFullAXTree` (per-frame — must be called once per frame and merged, it does not recurse into iframes on its own), `DOMSnapshot.captureSnapshot` (layout/style/attributes), and `Page.getLayoutMetrics` (viewport), producing `SnapshotNode`s keyed by `(loaderId, backendNodeId)` so refs survive DOM mutations.

  **What this changes about the plan:** the task description's "realistic path" (curl calls from inside the sandbox, same mechanism as Read/Bash) is still exactly right for session create/release and the stateless screenshot helper — cheap, and it's what should get built first. For navigate/act/snapshot/find, the realistic path is now: a small executable script (Node has a built-in `WebSocket` client in the runtime already available in the sandbox image; no new dependency needed) that opens ONE websocket connection to the freshly-fetched `websocketUrl`, sends exactly one CDP command, awaits the one matching response, prints it as JSON, and exits — run via the exact same `runCommand`-from-inside-the-sandbox mechanism Read/Bash already use, just executing a small script instead of a single `curl` invocation. This is still architecturally compatible with Gemini's one-shot `GeminiTool.execute()` shape (CDP does not require a *held-open* connection across calls — Steel's own browser process keeps the page/session alive between separate CDP connections, the same way `steel-mcp-server`'s own hosted mode serves one HTTP request at a time without keeping a socket open across requests) — but it is real new protocol-handling code, not a curl wrapper, and is real additional implementation and test surface beyond what "wire up 6 REST calls" implied. `steel_act`'s exact CDP method(s) (`Input.dispatchMouseEvent`/`dispatchKeyEvent`, or something higher-level) were not yet individually confirmed — the one remaining unread piece of `browse.ts`'s actual `act` implementation, not the architectural picture, which is now solid.

  Not yet started: writing the Gemini-side executors themselves (AC2-6). Given the scope this research surfaced is larger than "6 curl wrappers," flagging to the user before continuing rather than treating this as a same-pass continuation of TASK-226's scope-absorption precedent — a CDP client, however minimal, is a different category of build than a REST wrapper.
- [2026-09-09T05:40:00Z] [ORCH] RESOLVED, user confirmed "build all 6 now" after the research findings above. Built `createSteelGeminiTools` in `geminiToolExecutors.ts`: `mcp__steel__steel_session_create`/`_release` via `curl`; `_navigate`/`_snapshot`/`_act`/`_screenshot` via a small embedded Node script (`node -e`, global `WebSocket`) that opens one connection per tool call, runs a short command/event-wait sequence (e.g. navigate: `Page.enable` → `Page.navigate` → wait for `Page.loadEventFired` → `Runtime.evaluate` for title/text), and exits — the payload (which can carry model-supplied text) is base64-encoded into the trailing arg specifically to avoid shell-quoting it rather than trying to escape it. Every CDP call fetches a FRESH `websocketUrl` via `GET /v1/sessions/{id}` first, per the research note's own finding about token re-minting.

  Tool NAMES had to exactly match the manifest's `mcp__steel__*` literals (not bare `steel_navigate`) — traced `mountedToolNames`/`PolicyRegistry` construction in `chatRunDriver.ts` to confirm this before writing any tool, since a mismatched name would have meant the broker treated every call as undeclared rather than actually gating it.

  Two things caught and fixed that weren't in the original plan: (1) the shared outer catch in `runChatTask` that parks a run on a human-takeover signal had `actor` hardcoded to `"agent:claude"` — harmless while only the Claude lane could reach it, but wrong now that a `GeminiHumanTakeoverSignal` reaches the SAME catch; changed to the actual `effectiveProvider` (hoisted above the `try` so the `catch` block, a separate lexical scope, can read it). (2) The Steel tool's own `onHumanTakeover` callback originally ALSO recorded its own audit event (with `actor: "agent:gemini"` hardcoded there instead) — would have produced two events, one correctly and one incorrectly labelled, for the same detection. Removed that duplicate recording; the callback now only sets the flag, and the (now-correctly-labelled) outer catch is the single recorder. The new takeover integration test asserts exactly one event exists, specifically to catch a regression of either half of this fix.

  Documented two deliberate simplifications rather than claiming full upstream parity: `steel_snapshot` returns `Accessibility.getFullAXTree` + visible text, not upstream's full frame-tree/DOM-snapshot/layout-metrics merge (a genuinely large, unread file — see the research note); `steel_act` uses `Runtime.evaluate`-executed DOM manipulation (`.click()`, `.value` + events) rather than upstream's presumed synthetic `Input.dispatch*` — both real, working, CDP-based, neither confirmed byte-identical to `steel-mcp-server`'s own exact technique. Tightening either to exact parity is legitimate future work, not a blocker.

**Description:** Found during a discovery sweep for the "built, tested, never wired" defect class this session has now hit repeatedly (TASK-185, TASK-215 R1, TASK-220's own dispatch gap, TASK-224, TASK-225). `reconcileInterruptedRuns` is real, tested (`runLifecycle.test.ts`'s dedicated TASK-133 suite, plus `chatRunDriver.test.ts`'s TASK-136 approval-park test), and does exactly what a worker-crash-recovery routine should: scan for runs a task left non-terminal and resume them. Confirmed via `git grep`: its ONLY call sites anywhere in this repository are test files. It is not in `index.ts`'s export surface, so no other service (control-api included) even has a way to call it. `resumeInterruptedRun` (the single-run primitive it's built on) IS wired — used for the explicit, targeted resume case (e.g. an approval decision resuming one specific parked run) — so TARGETED resume works. What's missing is the BULK sweep: if the worker PROCESS ITSELF dies mid-turn (not "waiting for approval," but literally killed while a tool call was in flight), nothing ever finds and heals that run automatically. It stays stuck in whatever non-terminal state it was left in, forever, unless someone notices and manually intervenes.

**Title:** G-07 part 2a — make human take-over genuinely INTERACTIVE via execd's PTY holder mode (shell half only — CDP/browser half split to TASK-235)

**Owned_Paths:** — (investigation-first; likely `services/control-api/src/liveAgent.routes.ts` or a sibling takeoverRelay module, `services/control-api/src/ports.ts`/`index.ts` for real `LiveAgentPort`/`TakeoverPort` production wiring, `apps/mobile/lib/screens/live_agent_screen.dart` for an interactive mode, `packages/connectors/src/steelSession.ts` for the CDP handoff half — confirm real scope before widening)
**Depends_On:** TASK-188
**Description:** TASK-188 (G-07) shipped the real, tested park/hand-back backend and a functional take-over card — genuinely useful, genuinely done. What it deliberately did NOT ship, closing that task honestly rather than leaving it open against unresolved unknowns, is the part of G-07's own spec that makes take-over actually INTERACTIVE: the human driving the live session themselves (shell PTY and/or the Steel browser), not just being notified and later marking it complete. Two independent research passes (2026-09-07 and 2026-09-09) converged on the same conclusion: the underlying mechanism for the SHELL half genuinely exists and is well-understood now — execd's own PTY websocket (`/pty/{id}/ws`) defaults to an exclusive, write-capable "holder" mode (stdin/signals/resize), and a new connection can pass `takeover=1` to evict the current holder and become the new one, confirmed by reading execd's actual upstream source rather than guessing. What's still genuinely missing: (1) `LiveAgentPort`'s real production wiring doesn't exist yet even for the READ-ONLY case TASK-171 already built (`liveAgent.routes.ts`'s own header: deliberately left `undefined` in production, a deferred follow-up) — there's no live `role_sandboxes`-backed endpoint resolution to build an interactive path on top of; (2) the BROWSER half (Steel session handoff to the human's own WebSocket, the agent's CDP handle paused) has had zero research done — CDP has no obvious "holder eviction" primitive the way execd's PTY does, and needs its own investigation pass before any design; (3) the authorization/liveness-proof question TASK-188's earlier note raised is unanswered: TASK-171's `onInputDiscarded` mechanically PROVES a viewer connection's input never reaches execd (a real, tested security guarantee) — an interactive mode needs the mirror-image proof, that authorized take-over input DOES reach execd/Steel, and does NOT before authorization or after hand-back, with the same rigor. This is a real, security-relevant design question (ADR-010's enforced set exists precisely because a model must never see a password/2FA/CAPTCHA/payment step), not a routine feature build.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Real production wiring for `LiveAgentPort` (the read-only case TASK-171 already spec'd) OR confirmation it's covered elsewhere before this task duplicates effort — check first. RESOLVED, and this task's own Description was WRONG about it: `createDatabaseBackedLiveAgent` (`services/control-api/src/ports.ts`) IS genuinely wired into the real production entrypoint — `services/control-api/src/index.ts`'s `start()` (the exact function `dist/index.js` runs) passes `liveAgent: createDatabaseBackedLiveAgent(dbOptions)` into `buildApp`. `liveAgent.routes.ts`'s own header comment claiming this is "left `undefined` in production" was stale — confirmed by direct code trace, not by trusting the comment.
- [x] Shell/PTY interactive mode: a real connection using execd's holder-mode + `takeover=1` contract, with a liveness-proof test mirroring TASK-171's `onInputDiscarded` guarantee in the opposite direction. Built as a deliberately SEPARATE code path from the read-only viewer (`relayTakeover`/`handleTakeoverUpgrade`/`GET /roles/:roleId/live-agent/takeover`, mirroring `relay`/`handleUpgrade`/the viewer's own route exactly in structure) rather than a mode flag threaded through the existing one — a shared function with an "except when this flag is true" branch is exactly the shape of bug that turns "input can never reach execd before authorization" from a hard guarantee into a soft one. `LiveAgentPort.getPtyTakeoverEndpoint` (optional, so an older/view-only port implementation isn't broken) requests `mode=holder&takeover=1`, never `mode=viewer`. `onInputForwarded` is the mirror-image liveness assertion to `onInputDiscarded`, proving real input genuinely reaches execd rather than merely being coded to.
- [~] A real research pass on the Steel/CDP browser-handoff half — split out to **TASK-235** (new), since it is genuinely unresearched and architecturally separate from the shell/PTY mechanism (no CDP "holder eviction" primitive the way execd's PTY has one) — bundling it into this task would have meant either rushing untested design or leaving the shell half's real, working, well-tested build stuck behind it indefinitely.
- [x] `TakeoverCard.onTakeOver` (apps/mobile) opens a genuinely interactive view once built. New `TakeoverScreen` (write-capable terminal: real output display plus a real text input that sends real keystrokes) is exactly what a real `onTakeOver` should navigate to. Found while wiring this, and recorded honestly rather than silently fixed here (out of this task's own scope, TASK-188's own gap, not one this task created): **`TakeoverCard` itself is never actually rendered anywhere in the app** — `grep`-confirmed zero usages outside its own widget file and its own unit test. The card and its `onTakeOver` callback have no live caller for `TakeoverScreen` to be opened FROM yet. Folded into TASK-235 as a prerequisite, since wiring the card into chat is needed for either take-over half (shell or browser) to be reachable by a real user.
- [x] Full suites, lint, typecheck, flutter analyze/test clean.

### TASK-229
**Title:** control-api and worker have zero process supervision — both die on machine restart/logout/crash with no auto-recovery
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** critical
**Spec_References:** `services/worker/src/main.ts`'s own header comment ("There is, as of this file, still no container/compose entry that runs this — that is a deployment/ops concern this task deliberately leaves open"); live incident 2026-09-09 (this session): a user-reported bot ("jeff") sat unanswered because `control-api` was running a stale build and `worker` had never been started in this environment at all — confirmed directly via `tasklist`/process inspection, not inferred.
**Owned_Paths:** infra/compose/**, docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md (new)
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** Both `services/control-api` and `services/worker` currently exist only as bare foreground processes (`node dist/index.js` / `node dist/main.js`) started by hand in a terminal on a personal Windows dev workstation (Tailscale host `studyworkstation`). Neither has any supervisor: no auto-restart on crash, no start-on-boot, no health check, nothing. If the machine sleeps, restarts, the terminal closes, or nobody remembers to start them, the product is silently down until someone notices — exactly what happened this session. `worker` specifically has never had a real deployment path at all; it was built (TASK-226) with the entrypoint but nothing that keeps it running. Given the existing shared infra box (`clawsrv`, already hosting ~20 unrelated containers) and the R350/month budget ceiling, the likely right shape is real service management — either `pm2`/systemd on `clawsrv` or a docker-compose entry alongside the existing `infra/compose/office/**` pattern — rather than continuing to run production-facing processes as manually-launched terminal jobs on a personal workstation.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Decide and record the target deployment shape (pm2 vs systemd vs docker-compose, and which host) — a real product-scope/ops decision, not purely mechanical. DECIDED: neither — pm2 was tried first and rejected (see Progress_Notes: accepted both apps as `online` with 0 restarts yet neither ever bound a port or logged a line, reproducibly). Windows Task Scheduler running `infra/compose/service-watchdog.ps1` instead — native, no extra runtime dependency, scoped to this workstation (not a clawsrv/systemd migration, which stays a separate future decision).
- [x] Both `control-api` and `worker` restart automatically on crash and on host reboot, with no manual step. Scheduled Task `OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog`: triggers at logon + every 2 minutes indefinitely, checks control-api (port 3000) and worker (`dist/main.js` on the command line), starts whichever is missing.
- [x] A documented runbook (`docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md`) covering start/stop/status/logs for both services under the chosen supervisor.
- [x] A liveness assertion per CLAUDE.md's control-liveness rule — proven live TWICE: (1) both processes killed by PID, `service-watchdog.ps1` run directly, both restarted, `/health` responded again; (2) both killed again, `schtasks /Run /TN "OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog"` — the REAL scheduled task, not a manual script invocation — both restarted with correct env (`DATABASE_URL` etc.), `/health` responded again. A genuinely healthy pair re-checked produces zero restarts (idempotent, does not thrash).
- [x] The existing manual runbook note updated: `docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md` supersedes the mobile handover's old "must be started manually" instruction; cross-referenced there.

**Progress_Notes:**

Also discovered along the way, worth recording rather than silently working around: the local dev Postgres itself (`infra/compose/docker-compose.local.yml`) was down too when this session started — Docker Desktop wasn't running. Started it, brought the container up, confirmed prior data (jeff's real bot, 2727 roles) survived the recreate. A real, independent finding: even the DATABASE has zero supervision today; Docker Desktop's own "start on login" setting is the documented (manual, one-time) mitigation for that specific piece, recorded as a known limitation in the runbook rather than solved here (out of this task's Owned_Paths — Docker Desktop app settings, not this repo).

  pm2 attempt: installed via `npx pm2`, wrote `infra/compose/ecosystem.config.cjs` with absolute paths (pm2's relative-path `cwd` resolution proved unreliable on Windows — resolved against the wrong base directory on first attempt). Both apps came up `online`, 0 restarts — but neither ever bound a port (`netstat` showed nothing on 3000) nor produced one line of output across `.pm2/logs/*.log`, even after an explicit `pm2 restart`. Reproducible, not a fluke. Rejected; config file deleted rather than left as broken/misleading tooling.

  Real fix: `infra/compose/service-watchdog.ps1` (native PowerShell, no extra dependency) + Windows Scheduled Task `OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog` (`schtasks /Create ... /SC MINUTE /MO 2`; `Register-ScheduledTask` itself returned `Access is denied` even at `-RunLevel Limited` in this environment — the classic `schtasks` CLI form worked without elevation). A real bug was caught during verification: the worker health-check's first version matched `CommandLine -like "*worker*dist*main.js*"`, but a real process's `CommandLine` is literally `"...\node.exe" dist/main.js` — `"worker"` comes from the *working directory*, which `Win32_Process.CommandLine` does not include. That false negative spawned a SECOND, uncoordinated worker process alongside a real live one (confirmed by direct reproduction: two node.exe PIDs both running `dist/main.js`). Fixed to match `*dist*main.js*` alone (unambiguous — only worker has that entrypoint) and re-verified idempotent on a healthy pair afterward.

The live worker and the test suite now share one `worker.routine-poll` pg-boss singleton queue name in the same dev database; TASK-221's own root-cause writeup already describes this exact queue as fragile under concurrent access. Not a defect in this task's work — a real, new operational constraint TASK-229 successfully doing its job exposed: running the test suite while the real worker is alive is now a genuine hazard in this shared, uncleaned dev database (same root condition as TASK-231/TASK-162, not yet resolved by either).
**Artifacts:** infra/compose/service-watchdog.ps1, docs/runbooks/service-supervision.md, Windows Scheduled Task `OIKONOMOS-ServiceWatchdog` (host-level, not a repo file)
**Test_Evidence:** Two independent kill-and-revive cycles, the second through the actual deployed Scheduled Task (`schtasks /Run`), both confirmed via `/health` responding again and `tasklist`/`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` PID inspection. A genuinely healthy pair re-checked is idempotent (0 restarts, correct log lines). A real false-negative bug in the worker health check was caught and fixed during this verification, not before it.

### TASK-230
**Title:** No latency/performance monitoring exists for chat runs — user-reported slowness cannot currently be measured or diagnosed
**Status:** done
**Assigned_To:** TBD
**Priority:** high
**Spec_References:** `packages/db/src/runs.ts` (`runs` table already has `started_at`/`ended_at` per row — the raw data exists, nothing reads it for this purpose); user report 2026-09-09 ("when this thing eventually comes up and I ask a question, it usually takes a long time for it to come back with an answer").
**Owned_Paths:** services/control-api/src/metrics.routes.ts (new), packages/db/src/runMetrics.ts (new), apps/dashboard/src/pages/ (metrics view, if in scope)
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** There is currently no visibility into how long a real chat run takes end to end — no logging, no dashboard, no alerting. Investigated 2026-09-09 while diagnosing an unrelated outage: every `runs` row currently in the database is a sub-second test-fixture double from automated test suites, not real LLM traffic, so there is no existing data to even retroactively analyze. Candidate contributors identified by reading the code (not yet measured): the default provider lane is FreeLLMAPI (cost-driven, likely slower/rate-limited than a paid lane), `CapabilityRegistry.build()` reloads connector manifests and re-reads the capability registry from the database on every single run with no caching, and the mobile client polls for new messages rather than receiving a live token stream, which can make a genuinely fast reply feel slow. This task is to instrument first, then optimize against real numbers rather than guesses.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Every run records enough to compute wall-clock latency broken down by phase (manifest/registry load, connector resolution, model call itself, DB writes) — not just total `started_at`→`ended_at`. New `run_phase_timings` table (migration `022_run_phase_timings`), three phases recorded per run: `setup` (manifests + capability registry + all connector resolution + role/run resolution), `model_execution` (whichever provider branch actually ran — Gemini, sandbox, or local queryFn), `finalize` (insertMessage + spend accounting + compaction + completeTaskRun).
- [x] A queryable surface (API endpoint and/or dashboard view) showing recent run latencies, p50/p95, and by-provider breakdown. `packages/db`'s `queryRunLatencyStats` (Postgres `percentile_cont`, not JS-side percentiles) + `GET /internal/run-latency` on control-api (optional-deps pattern, matching this file's existing `listSkills`-style 501 fallback so the many pre-existing test-fixture `ControlApiDeps` objects didn't all need updating).
- [x] At least one real measurement of a genuine end-to-end chat run's latency, broken down by phase, recorded in this task's Progress_Notes as a baseline — see below.
- [x] A liveness assertion proving the instrumentation itself is live, not just present in code — new in-source test in `chatRunDriver.ts` runs a real chat turn against real Postgres and asserts real `setup`/`model_execution`/`finalize` rows landed for that run's actual `run_id`, each ≥0ms. Passing.

**Status:** done

**Owned_Paths:** infra/postgres/**, scripts/db-cleanup.* (new)
**Depends_On:** —
**Description:** This session's own `pnpm -r test` run, like apparently many before it, created real rows (roles, threads, tasks, runs) in the shared dev Postgres instance rather than an isolated/transactional test database, and nothing ever cleans them up. Confirmed harmless today — nothing currently consumes runs sitting in `resumed` status automatically — but it pollutes query results (as seen investigating TASK-229/this session), makes manual DB inspection harder, and is the same underlying condition implicated in TASK-162's flaky-test investigation. Two halves: (1) a one-time cleanup of the current backlog, (2) a structural fix so test runs stop writing permanent rows into a database anyone can query — either a dedicated test-tenant convention with a scheduled purge, or moving DB-backed tests to a genuinely ephemeral database per run.
**Acceptance_Criteria:**
- [x] Confirm no cleanup touches genuinely real (non-test-fixture) rows — a clear, defensible rule for identifying test fixtures before deleting anything. RULE (deliberately conservative — see Progress_Notes for why a UUID-shaped role_id was tried first and rejected): a row is a fixture only if its `tenant_id` matches the literal shape `task-<digits>-<uuid>`, the per-test isolation convention this repo's own suites construct. Real production roles use either a real Firebase UID or the literal constant `"basileia"` — never that shape. Under-deleting is the accepted failure mode, not over-deleting.
- [x] One-time cleanup of the current backlog, with a before/after row count recorded in Progress_Notes. Done — see below. `roles: 2727 → 2229`, jeff and maestro (real bots) confirmed still present by direct query afterward.
- [x] A structural fix so `pnpm -r test` stops accumulating permanent rows in the shared dev database going forward. Root `package.json` `posttest` script now runs the same cleanup script (`--execute`, `|| true` so a cleanup hiccup never fails the actual test run) automatically after every `pnpm test`/`pnpm -r test`.
- [x] Cross-reference with TASK-162 — see TASK-229's own Progress_Notes for a NEW, related finding this task's cleanup did not resolve: a live worker process and the test suite now contend for the same pg-boss queue in this same shared, uncleaned database. TASK-162 itself not independently re-verified this session (out of scope tonight); this task's conservative selection rule deliberately does not touch the `"basileia"`-tenant rows, so TASK-162's original real-Postgres flake may still reproduce for reasons this cleanup doesn't address.
**Branch:** —
**Started_At:** 2026-09-09T17:21:00Z
**Progress_Notes:**
- [2026-09-09T17:21:00Z] [ORCH] Filed after discovering the 6,124-row backlog while diagnosing TASK-229's outage. Deliberately not attempted as a quick fix in that session — deleting rows from a shared database without a verified selection rule is exactly the kind of state change CLAUDE.md's incident-disclosure history in this file's own orchestrator_notes warns against doing unannounced.
- [2026-09-11T20:30:00Z] [ORCH] RESOLVED at a deliberately conservative scope. First candidate rule (role_id shaped like a UUID vs. a human-readable slug) was tested and REJECTED before any delete ran: direct query showed 1,713 of 2,727 roles had UUID-shaped role_ids, but many of those were ALSO test fixtures (e.g. `"Handoff recipient <uuid>"`, `"Revoke grants <uuid>"` — test code that generates a real UUID for role_id but a descriptive name) — role_id shape alone is not a reliable signal. `tenant_id` grouped cleanly instead: `"basileia"` (1,736 rows, the real production convention per `main.ts`'s own `DEFAULT_TENANT_ID` comment) vs. real Firebase UIDs (jeff's tenant, 4 rows) vs. ~166 distinct `task-<N>-<uuid>` tenants (unambiguously test-only — real users never get a tenant_id in that shape). Went with the tenant_id rule.

  New `scripts/db-cleanup.mjs`: computes the target tenant set, deletes in FK-dependency order (derived from a live `information_schema` query against every FK referencing `roles`/`tasks`/`runs`/`threads` — 15 tables, children before parents) inside ONE transaction, dry-run by default (`--execute` to commit). `pg` added as a root `devDependency` (wasn't hoisted to root `node_modules` under pnpm's strict linking; a plain `node scripts/db-cleanup.mjs` failed with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` until this was added).

  Dry run first: 498 fixture roles, 161 runs, 168 tasks/threads, 158 messages, 84 role_grants, 161 role_messages — zero touching `"basileia"` or any real Firebase-tenant row. Executed for real: `roles: 2727 → 2229`. Verified afterward: jeff and maestro (real bots) both still present by direct query.

  Structural fix: added `posttest` to root `package.json` (`node scripts/db-cleanup.mjs --execute || true`) — npm/pnpm's own pre/post script convention fires it automatically after `pnpm test`/`pnpm -r test`, no CI/workflow change needed. Confirmed later in this same session that new test runs DO still accumulate rows under the `"basileia"` tenant (the conservative rule's known, accepted gap) — after several more `pnpm -r test` runs tonight, `reconcileInterruptedRuns` reported 6,178 open runs, UP from the post-cleanup baseline despite the posttest hook running each time, because those newer rows are `"basileia"`-tenant and this rule deliberately never touches that tenant. Recorded honestly rather than claimed as fully solved: the backlog is now BOUNDED (safely-identifiable fixtures no longer accumulate) but not ELIMINATED (the shared, ambiguous `"basileia"` tenant still grows). A future task could pursue per-test-file tenant randomization (moving fixtures off the `"basileia"` literal entirely) as the real fix for that remainder — out of scope tonight.
**Artifacts:** scripts/db-cleanup.mjs, package.json (`posttest` script, `pg` devDependency)
**Test_Evidence:** Dry run and executed run both captured in Progress_Notes with exact before/after counts. Real bots (jeff, maestro) confirmed present post-cleanup via direct query. `node scripts/db-cleanup.mjs` (no `--execute`) re-run afterward reports 0 fixture-shaped tenants remaining from the ORIGINAL backlog (new ones from this session's own subsequent test runs are a separate, expected, documented gap above).

Today `ChatPage.tsx:116` and `ChatShell.tsx:54-64` each own `activeBotId`; the parent's `handleSelectBot` (`ChatPage.tsx:177-191`) never calls its own setter, so the SSE effect (`ChatPage.tsx:219-253`) and the routines lookup stay on the first thread while the child renders another. `isBotResponding`/`pendingSinceRef` are one value for all threads (`ChatPage.tsx:119,125,179-181`). `ComposeBox` holds one draft, never remounts on switch, and clears before the void `handleSend` resolves (`ComposeBox.tsx:18-25`, `ChatPage.tsx:297`), so a failed POST loses the text. `ChatPage.tsx:292` passes `members={[]}` and the Members tab is the right panel's default, so it is permanently empty; the sidebar's create-bot dialog works but the thread list is never refreshed after creation.

Merge messages by id and never let a slower history fetch overwrite streamed messages. Add `/workspace/:threadId` in `App.tsx`; `/` redirects to the most recent thread. Fetch the roster (`listRoles()` already returns it — `ChatPage.tsx:153` discards it) and refresh threads after create. **Description:** Three small routes and one bounded projection. Derive `latestRun` from the thread's newest `messages.run_id` joined to `runs`, and `pendingApprovals` from `approvals` with `status='pending'` on that run — no new association table. Put the SQL in `packages/db/src/workspaceSummary.ts` behind a port on `ChatDependencies` in `ports.ts` (interface + database-backed implementation only; do not touch the `runChatTask` composition at `ports.ts:393`, TASK-238 owns that next). (d) `GET /health` gains `buildSha` (read from `OIKONOMOS_BUILD_SHA` env or `git rev-parse` at start, never at request time). (e) Replace the stale paragraph at `liveAgent.routes.ts:35-44` that says production wiring is deferred — `index.ts:42` wires it; this is a comment-only edit in that file. Tests go in new files (`session.routes.test.ts`, `workspace.routes.test.ts`) — `chat.routes.test.ts` belongs to blocked TASK-162, do not edit it. 404-never-403 discipline throughout.
